_comment: Expected compliance verdicts, hand-determined from the stored records. Only requirement/asset pairs whose answer is definite are listed: interval arithmetic against dated inspection records, and graph state. Requirements testable only by reading procedure text or permit records are deliberately excluded -- their correct verdict is 'a human must decide', and grading the system on agreeing with a judgement nobody has made would be circular. Determined against a corpus whose latest inspection is 2025-05-27; the overdue verdicts below assume evaluation after 2026-06-26 (the 12-month interval plus the 30-day grace).

notes: Internal inspection or equivalent, 48-month interval. Last recorded 2025-05-27, so next due 2029-05-27 -- comfortably current.
Thickness readings against fixed CMLs, no interval stated. Twelve readings exist against CML-01/02/03, so the obligation is met by the records existing.
External visual inspection, 12-month interval. Last recorded 2025-05-27, due 2026-05-27, and the evaluation date is past that plus the grace period.
Pressure plant examination, 12-month interval. Same arithmetic as OISD-128-6.1-a and therefore the same verdict.

Corrected after the first benchmark run. OISD-128 scopes to equipment class 'V' (pressure vessel) and E-104 is class 'E' (heat exchanger), so the clause does not bite on it. The system was right and this expectation was wrong -- a heat exchanger is a pressure envelope in engineering practice, but the loaded requirement says 'V' and scoping to what the requirement actually says is the correct behaviour. Widening the class would be a data change, not a code fix.

MOC-2023-07 altered P-101B and the documents describing it were not revised afterwards. This is the change-control gap the graph-state evaluator exists to find, and it is a real finding: the MOC itself records that the datasheet and P&ID were not updated.
No approved change alters V-102, so no document can be stale relative to one. Included to check the evaluator distinguishes 'no violation' from 'not checked'.

A pressure-vessel clause evaluated against a pump. Correctly out of scope -- and reporting it as a gap would be a category error, which is how compliance dashboards come to show hundreds of meaningless findings.
Hot-work permit validity, testable only against permit records. No permit system is connected, so the honest verdict is unexamined -- neither satisfied nor breached.

Machine guarding. The system holds no record type that evidences it, and absent thickness readings say nothing about whether a coupling guard is fitted. Regression guard for a bug that reported this as a breach.
